operational_interpretation: Direct operational volume coupling; schedules predict 98% of physical movements.
Direct delay propagation downline; en-route flight schedule padding absorbs less than 8.3% of delay.
Severe collinearity; average delay minutes scale almost 1:1 with delayed flight counts.
Surface queue coupling; late gate pushbacks and GDP metering create congested runway queues.
Surface-to-air delay feedback; delayed departure banks create severe tarmac taxi congestion.
Shared exogenous shock overlap; severe storm events cause both extended delays and tactical cancellations.
Hub scale penalty; higher scheduled flight volume increases exposure to network cascading delays.
Disruption threshold effect; cascading delay networks eventually trigger tactical cancellations.
Schedule density increases delay risk, but delay magnitude is dominated by weather and FAA GDP shocks.
Departure bank saturation; heavily scheduled departure banks induce surface taxi sequencing queues.
Weak surface queue cancellation coupling; airlines avoid cancellations from tarmac delays due to 3-hr rule.
Slight fortress resilience; larger hub carriers prioritize completing scheduled mainline flights over cancellations.
Internal operational disruption; carrier-controllable crew/mechanical issues drive 43% of delay variance.
Network propagation cascade; late inbound aircraft arrival drives 33% of departure delay variance.
Severe meteorological shock; localized extreme weather creates high kurtosis delay spikes.
Airspace congestion programs; FAA ground delay programs primarily manifest in taxi-out queues.
